strengths: Clearly identifies and motivates a real gap—Instruction-Visual (IV) Complexity—where cluttered scenes and reasoning-heavy instructions cause existing unified VLM+diffusion editors to fail at fine-grained grounding, and supports this with convincing qualitative examples.

The RePlan architecture is well-motivated: rather than treating the VLM as a coarse semantic encoder, it produces explicit region-hint pairs and enforces them via a training-free, interpretable attention-masking scheme (intra-group, hint isolation, image-latent full interaction, region/background constraints) that enables parallel multi-region edits without iterative inpainting, avoiding compounding degradation.

Reasonable resource efficiency: GRPO fine-tuning of the planner uses only ~1K instruction-only samples (no paired ground-truth images needed), yet yields consistent gains over base Flux.1 Kontext and Qwen-Image-Edit backbones, and outperforms several baselines trained on much larger data.

Thorough ablation suite: comparison of zero-shot planners (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen2.5-VL) vs. the RL-trained planner, reasoning (CoT) removal ablation, two-stage vs. single-stage RL ablation, bounding-box perturbation robustness (up to 50%), and handling of overlapping regions — these substantially strengthen the soundness case for individual design choices.

Introduces IV-Edit, a new benchmark explicitly targeting referring-expression diversity (feature/spatial/knowledge/understanding referring, text visual/structural/content referring) and diverse task types (including reasoning-based, prediction, physics/scenario reasoning, text edits), with reasonably detailed construction/filtering pipeline described in the appendix.
Appendix includes useful supplementary analyses (attention-rule ablations in Figs. 9–11, qualitative failure/success illustrations) that add insight into why the attention-injection mechanism works.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol relies entirely on a single automatic VLM judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro) for all four scoring dimensions; no human evaluation or correlation study is provided to validate that these automatic scores track human judgments of edit quality, which is a significant reproducibility/soundness concern given the benchmark and results are central contributions.

The IV-Edit benchmark (~800 instruction-image pairs) and its automatic quality-control pipeline are constructed using Gemini-2.5-Pro (for filtering, instruction generation, and ambiguity removal), the same model family used later as the evaluation judge — this overlap raises a potential circularity/self-consistency bias that is not discussed or mitigated.

Despite the proposed improvements, RePlan's absolute Overall/Weighted scores (e.g., 3.22–3.51) remain clearly below strong proprietary baselines like Gemini-Flash-Image (3.71) and are only modestly ahead of the base open-source backbones—so the paper mainly demonstrates relative gains for open-source models rather than closing the gap with best available systems; this should be more directly acknowledged as a limitation.

No analysis of inference-time/computational overhead introduced by the two-stage plan-then-execute pipeline (VLM reasoning + region parsing + modified attention masks) relative to single-pass baselines, which is relevant for an 'Applied/Systems'-flavored contribution claiming efficiency benefits over iterative inpainting.

Benchmark scale (~800 samples, cross 7 referring types and 16 task types) is relatively small, and some categories (e.g., Open-Ended Reasoning with 6 samples) contain too few samples for statistically meaningful per-category conclusions; per-category breakdowns of RePlan's performance are not shown in the main text.

The paper does not report failure-mode statistics (e.g., cases where the VLM planner mis-identifies the number/location of regions, not just bbox coordinate noise), leaving open how robust the system is to target-identification errors rather than just localization-perturbation errors already tested.

strengths: Clear problem formulation (IV-Complexity) that identifies a real and underexplored gap in instruction-based editing: performance degradation under cluttered scenes and complex referring instructions.

The training-free attention region injection mechanism is a reasonably elegant way to achieve parallel, multi-region, mask-free editing within a single MMDiT forward pass, avoiding the error accumulation of iterative inpainting pipelines.

Good engineering and ablation coverage: comparisons of zero-shot planners (Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen2.5-VL) vs. the GRPO-trained planner, reasoning on/off ablation, one-stage vs. two-stage RL ablation, bbox perturbation robustness test, and overlapping-box handling are all reported, which supports the internal logic of the design.

Data efficiency claim is interesting: only ~1k instruction-only examples are used for RL fine-tuning of the planner, which, if reliable, is a meaningful practical advantage over methods requiring large paired datasets.

The appendix's attention-rule discovery experiments (Figs. 9-11) provide some mechanistic insight into why each masking rule is necessary, improving interpretability of the design choices rather than presenting them as ad hoc.
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to results: the abstract/intro claim RePlan 'consistently outperforms' baselines, but Table 1 shows RePlan trails strong closed-source models (Gemini-Flash-Image, GPT-4o) and even some open-source competitors on Quality/Target/Effect; the gains are concentrated mainly in Consistency and the derived Overall/Weighted scores, which are themselves defined by the authors. This creates a risk that the headline metric is tuned to favor the proposed method's known strength (avoiding spillover) rather than reflecting balanced superiority.

Evaluation circularity concern: the IV-Edit benchmark is constructed using Gemini-2.5-Pro (for image filtering and instruction construction) and evaluated using Gemini-2.5-Pro as the automatic judge, and the GRPO reward model is also VLM-based (Qwen2.5-VL-72B). There is no human evaluation or inter-rater reliability analysis reported to validate that the automatic scores track genuine edit quality, which weakens confidence in the quantitative claims.

Benchmark scale is modest (~800 instruction-image pairs) and built from a narrow set of sources (COCO, LISA ReasonSeg, TextSceneHQ, TableVQA-Bench, TableQA); no cross-validation on existing established benchmarks (MagicBrush, ImgEdit, GEdit, KrisBench, RISEBench) is provided to show the method's advantage generalizes beyond the authors' own curated test set, raising concerns about selection bias in benchmark design relative to the proposed method's strengths.

The method is only demonstrated on two backbones (Flux.1 Kontext dev and Qwen-Image-Edit), both sharing the MMDiT architecture; generalization of the attention-region-injection technique to other architectures (e.g., UNet-based diffusion editors) is not shown, limiting claims of broad applicability.

The approach's accuracy is fundamentally bottlenecked by the VLM planner's bounding-box grounding; while a synthetic bbox-perturbation robustness test is included, it does not address realistic VLM failure modes (e.g., completely wrong region selection, omitted targets, hallucinated referents), which are arguably the dominant source of error in real deployments and are not quantitatively characterized.

Claims of outperforming 'models trained on orders of magnitude more data' are not accompanied by a clear, quantified comparison of training data/compute scale for each baseline, making the efficiency claim more rhetorical than substantiated.

Technical novelty is incremental: regional attention masking/grouping for localized diffusion generation is a known idea in controllable image generation/editing literature, and the core contribution here is largely an engineering combination (VLM reasoning + region-gated attention + GRPO formatting rewards) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; the paper could better position its specific technical advance relative to prior regional-control diffusion work.

strengths: Clearly motivates and formalizes a real, underexplored problem (Instruction-Visual Complexity) that captures the interaction between cluttered scenes, fine-grained referring expressions, and knowledge-based reasoning in instruction-based editing.

The training-free attention region injection mechanism is a simple but well-designed idea: it turns VLM region-aligned guidance into precise per-region control within an MMDiT without additional inpainting rounds, and the appendix ablations (E, F, G) convincingly dissect the role of each attention rule (hint isolation, region constraint, background constraint, image-latent interaction) and show the method handles overlapping boxes and is robust to substantial bbox perturbation (up to 50-70%).

Efficient training recipe: the two-stage GRPO scheme uses only ~1K instruction-only samples yet yields a planner that outperforms much more heavily-trained end-to-end unified editing models, and the paper includes clean ablations isolating the effect of reasoning (CoT) and the staged RL design versus a single-stage baseline.

IV-Edit benchmark is constructed with a thoughtful taxonomy (7 referring types x 16 task types), a documented multi-stage filtering pipeline (image filtering, instruction construction, bbox-based instruction filtering, manual verification), and is applied consistently to compare 8 baselines including strong proprietary systems (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Flash-Image).

Qualitative results across many diverse examples (main paper and Appendix H) support the quantitative claims, showing reduced spillover into semantically similar regions and correct handling of implicit/indirect references (e.g., inferring 'July' from 'June').
weaknesses: The entire evaluation protocol depends on a single automatic judge (Gemini-2.5-Pro for the benchmark, Qwen2.5-VL-72B for the RL reward), with no human study or correlation analysis to validate that these VLM-based scores track actual editing quality; this is a significant reproducibility/validity concern given that the paper's central claims rest on these scores.

There is a degree of circularity/self-reinforcement in the pipeline: VLM-family models (Qwen2.5-VL, Gemini-2.5-Pro) are used both to construct/filter the benchmark (bbox annotation, instruction filtering) and to score the outputs, and the same Qwen2.5-VL backbone is used as the RePlan planner, which could bias results in RePlan's favor in ways not fully controlled for.

RePlan's benefit is inconsistent across backbones: with Qwen-Image-Edit, RePlan raises Overall/Weighted scores but Consistency remains very low (1.79) and Effect is comparable to the base model, suggesting the gains are backbone-dependent and not uniformly explained; this nuance is not discussed in depth.

No explicit limitations section or discussion of failure modes (e.g., cases with many overlapping/conflicting instructions, extremely small regions, or planner hallucination beyond the bbox-perturbation robustness check), despite space being available in the appendix.

No computational cost / inference-time comparison is reported for the added VLM planning + attention-injection pipeline versus baseline single-pass diffusion editors, which matters for assessing practical impact.

The benchmark is modest in scale (~800 instruction-image pairs), and while categorization is thorough, per-category breakdowns of results (e.g., performance by referring type or task type) are not shown, limiting insight into where the method's advantages and remaining weaknesses lie.
